items.title: Junior Mance Part II interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 18, 1999 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: we had a great bass player in Dizzy’s band at the time, we had Sam Jones

ctx.x: Well you’re mentioning Gene Ammons reminds me — I wanted to ask you about — for the first part of your career you were playing with different combos and stuff. And eventually you got to a point where you started becoming your own leader, of your trio.

Yeah. That was years later though after Gene Ammons. I think it was about 1961 that I gave serious thought to becoming a leader. Because I made my first record as a leader in ’58 or ’59, it was a Verve record called “Just Plain Junior.” I was playing with Dizzy at the time. And Norman Granz, who then was the owner of Verve records, was also the producer. So he came out of the booth during the break and said, “How would you like to do your own album?” And I was speechless. I didn’t know what to say. Finally I said…
Yeah. I have that CD you mentioned.

items.title: 68533_Sam Jones oral history interview
items.q: And I--they had Junior Mance on the piano. Phew. And that was an experience. And JimmyCobb on the drums and myself, rhythm section.

ctx.x: I was gigging round town then, you know. Been playing little gigs, small time dances uptown and them little club dates and stuff. So Cannon come to town and wanted me to play in the band. And I--they had Junior Mance on the piano. Phew. And that was an experience. And JimmyCobb on the drums and myself, rhythm section. But the band--it was alright. We travelled around and the band never got off the ground. You know what I mean. Never could make no money, you know.
You say with Junior that was--would you say that was really--

items.title: Junior Mance Part I interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, New York City, New York, July 27, 1995…
items.q: We had a great bass player too, Sam Jones was the bass player that Dizzy really loved and who I was going to use anyway.

ctx.x: With myself? I could be. That’s what everybody says. But I don’t know why I’m like that. I listen to my records like in the studio and I may listen to like the rough draft of it,

like when they give you the cassettes to take home. But when it comes out I never listen to it. I may hear it by accident like on WBGO you know, the jazz station, or something like that. But I don’t play them at home. I never listen to them. I know, when you said about being overly critical, I think I might be because I used to always, I remember when I first started recording I would say now why did I do that? Why didn’t I do such-and- such a thing? The only record I really liked that I ever made was my first…
